strengths: The manuscript studies a relevant problem: extracting naturally occurring feedback from multi-turn user–LLM conversations for preference training. The proposed pipeline is intuitive and potentially useful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/a0a252b41557454fb5ad90e79e91163a/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The dataset is reasonably substantial, and the paper evaluates three open-weight model families on several established instruction-following benchmarks.
The authors validate feedback-signal classification against expert annotations and report accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and agreement. The reported human–human agreement also gives useful context.
Prompts, rubric definitions, dataset statistics, and core SFT/DPO hyperparameters are documented, and the paper candidly acknowledges selection bias and potentially harmful user preferences.
Models trained on the GPT-4-generated version improve consistently on AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard, and MT-Bench, indicating that the resulting training data has practical utility.
weaknesses: The experiments do not establish the central causal claim that in-situ feedback is responsible for the improvements. The strongest results come from GPT-4-generated preferred responses, but there is no matched GPT-4 distillation baseline without user-derived preference summaries, nor comparisons with UltraFeedback or other standard alignment datasets under the same training budget. The gains may therefore reflect ordinary GPT-4 distillation rather than the proposed feedback mechanism.

The proposed evaluation is substantially circular: GPT-4 extracts the preference checklist, that checklist conditions generation of preferred responses, and GPT-4 then judges responses using the same checklist. Figure 2 consequently does not independently validate that the constructed preferences or responses match users. No human evaluation tests the generated response pairs or the claimed superiority of checklist-guided judging.

The satisfaction labels are imperfect proxies for preferences. Revision requests can be normal iterative specification rather than dissatisfaction, while gratitude and continued engagement do not necessarily endorse the preceding response. Validation covers only 50 conversations; DSAT recall is 48.4%, GPT–human κ is 0.50, and human–human κ is only 0.54. This moderate reliability is not propagated into an analysis of dataset noise or downstream performance.

The user-guided test set is not convincingly representative of broader human preferences. It deliberately selects preferences most similar to others within each prompt cluster, uses post-hoc feedback unavailable at the original query, and is derived from the same source corpus and GPT-4 extraction process as training. Selecting ten items per cluster also does not demonstrate that the resulting distribution represents a population majority.

Several conclusions are overstated. The evidence supports neither alignment with “true human values” nor resolution of subjectivity and bias: WildChat users are a self-selected population, dissatisfied users are overrepresented, preferences are mediated by GPT-4, and harmful or conflicting values receive only a simple safety instruction and moderation filter.

The on-policy evidence is mixed: Mistral deteriorates on all three public benchmarks, Phi 3 is essentially unchanged on length-controlled AlpacaEval, and other improvements are sometimes small. There are no multiple runs, confidence intervals, significance tests, or robustness analyses, so the reliability of these differences is unclear.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate for Findings. The dataset is only promised as “available soon,” and no code or checkpoints are provided. Important details are missing, including exact splits and filtering counts, decoding settings for data generation, random seeds, optimizer and adaptation configuration, sequence lengths, moderation criteria, clustering embeddings and parameters, and the full hyperparameter search protocol.

The paper does not adequately address privacy, consent, memorization, or licensing risks arising from training on real conversation logs that may contain personal or sensitive information. Overall, the idea is promising, but independent human validation and controlled baselines are needed before the central claims are sufficiently sound for publication.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: exploiting naturally occurring user feedback rather than relying entirely on commissioned preference labels or synthetic critiques.

The proposed pipeline is intuitive and practically motivated, combining feedback-signal detection, preference-pair construction, and preference-conditioned evaluation on a substantial corpus of multi-turn conversations.

The GPT-4-generated version produces large gains across three established instruction-following benchmarks and three open-weight model families, suggesting that the resulting training data is useful, even though the source of those gains is not adequately isolated.

The authors validate SAT/DSAT classification against adjudicated human annotations, report precision, recall, F1, and agreement, separate evaluation users from training users, and provide prompts and basic training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central attribution is unsupported. Preferred responses in the strongest condition are generated by GPT-4, models receive GPT-4 SFT followed by DPO, and evaluation also uses GPT-4. There is no size-matched generic GPT-4-distillation baseline, checklist-free generation control, alternative preference dataset baseline, or SFT-versus-DPO ablation. Consequently, the reported gains cannot be attributed specifically to in-situ user feedback rather than ordinary GPT-4 distillation and judge self-preference.

The claimed alignment with real users or “true human values” is not established. No actual users evaluate the trained models, and human annotators do not validate the extracted preference summaries or preferred responses. Instead, GPT-4 summarizes preferences, generates preferred answers, filters examples, and judges outcomes using those same summaries, creating a strongly circular construction and evaluation procedure.

The custom WILDFEEDBACK evaluation is particularly vulnerable to leakage by construction: test cases are selected around automatically summarized preferences, and the same type of preference checklist is supplied to the GPT-4 judge. This primarily demonstrates conformity to GPT-4's interpretation of a checklist, not improved user satisfaction. Reporting results without the checklist does not fix the GPT-4-generation and GPT-4-judge confound.

Feedback identification is only weakly validated: the test set contains merely 50 conversations, DSAT human-human agreement is modest (κ=0.54), and GPT-4's DSAT recall is only 48.4%. The paper nevertheless treats the automatically labeled corpus as reliable and makes no attempt to quantify how this label noise affects the dataset or downstream findings.

The data-construction description is incomplete and internally ambiguous. It does not clearly explain how SAT cases yield preferred/dispreferred pairs, despite presenting SAT as a core signal. Exact selection and filtering rules, moderation losses, sampling parameters, split sizes, FAISS embedding model and clustering settings, deduplication procedure, and complete response-generation configuration are missing.

Several conclusions contradict the evidence. The claim that training does not compromise benchmark performance is false for on-policy Mistral, which declines on every reported public benchmark; Phi-3 also slightly declines on length-controlled AlpacaEval. No confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated runs, or variance estimates are provided, so claims of significant and consistent improvement are not statistically supported.

The source population is highly selected and demographically unknown, while dissatisfied users are overrepresented. Treating this population as representative of broad human values is unjustified. The paper also lacks an adequate ethics and privacy discussion for repurposing real conversational logs and deriving latent user preferences.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate for Findings: the manuscript says only that the dataset “will be available soon,” supplies no code or artifact link, and omits essential processing and evaluation details. The work needs controlled baselines, independent human evaluation, uncertainty analysis, a precise end-to-end specification, and an accessible artifact before its main claims can be assessed reliably. strengths: The paper addresses an important and highly relevant NLP problem: extracting preference supervision from naturally occurring, multi-turn user–LLM interactions rather than relying entirely on purpose-built annotations.

WILDFEEDBACK is a coherent end-to-end framework covering feedback detection, preference-pair construction, training, and user-guided evaluation. The paper clearly documents the prompts, SAT/DSAT taxonomy, annotation procedure, dataset statistics, and principal training hyperparameters.

The use of 148,715 WildChat conversations yields a potentially valuable resource of 20,281 multi-turn preference examples. User-level and conversation-level separation between training and evaluation data is an important safeguard against direct leakage.

Validation by four expert annotators provides some evidence for the feedback-identification stage. GPT-4 agreement is substantial for SAT detection, and the paper transparently reports the weaker DSAT results.

Experiments cover three open models and several established instruction-following benchmarks. Training on the GPT-4-generated version produces large, consistent gains across AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard, MT-Bench, and the proposed evaluation, supporting the practical usefulness of the resulting data.
The limitations section appropriately acknowledges selection bias and the risk of learning malicious or otherwise undesirable user preferences.
weaknesses: The central attribution to authentic user feedback is not isolated experimentally. GPT-4 identifies feedback, summarizes preferences, generates the preferred responses, and judges many outcomes. The strong GPT-4-version results may therefore primarily reflect GPT-4 distillation or additional SFT data rather than the value of in-situ preferences. A size-matched control using GPT-4 responses generated without extracted preferences, and comparisons with established preference datasets under identical training settings, are needed.

The proposed evaluation is substantially circular: GPT-4-derived preference summaries guide GPT-4 judging, and the GPT-4 dataset was generated from those same summaries. Providing a checklist can mechanically favor checklist-conditioned responses. No direct human evaluation establishes that the reported model wins correspond to the originating users' intentions or to independent human judgments.

The evidence for feedback-label quality is limited to 50 conversations. Human–human agreement is only moderate for DSAT (κ=0.54), GPT–human agreement is κ=0.50, and DSAT recall is 48.4%. Because DSAT examples are central to constructing preference pairs, these errors could materially affect dataset validity, yet no downstream sensitivity or error analysis is provided.

Claims that the method improves alignment with “true human values,” represents the broader population, or resolves subjectivity are too strong. WildChat users are a selected and potentially unrepresentative population; only users who provide detectable textual feedback contribute; dissatisfaction is overrepresented; and selecting cluster-central evaluation examples further suppresses minority preferences.

The on-policy evidence is mixed: Mistral degrades on every standard benchmark, while gains for Phi-3 and LLaMA 3 are smaller or inconsistent. Thus the most convincing improvements come from the confounded GPT-4-generated condition rather than from a clean test of learning from natural feedback.

The empirical analysis lacks uncertainty estimates, significance testing, multiple training seeds, and systematic qualitative error analysis. This makes it difficult to assess the robustness of relatively small differences and judge failure modes.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate for a clear Findings recommendation: the dataset is only promised as “available soon,” no code or release artifact is identified, important generation and filtering details are underspecified, and the proprietary GPT-4 and moderation-API components are version-dependent.

Safety and ethics treatment is incomplete for a dataset derived from real user conversations. A generic “response should be safe” instruction and an opaque moderation filter do not establish safety, while privacy, consent, demographic/language coverage, annotator conditions, and harmful-preference audit results are not discussed in sufficient depth.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, well-motivated NLP problem: exploiting naturally occurring feedback in multi-turn conversations instead of relying exclusively on commissioned annotations or fully synthetic preference labels.

The proposed pipeline—feedback detection, preference extraction, pair construction, and checklist-guided evaluation—is coherent and practically useful. It produces a sizable multi-turn resource and explicitly considers harmful preferences, privacy, and selection bias.

Experiments span three model families and compare both GPT-4-generated and on-policy data against instruction-tuned and UltraFeedback baselines. Improvements over the base models across AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard, and MT-Bench provide credible evidence that the resulting data can improve general instruction-following performance.

The authors validate feedback classification with expert annotations, disclose class-specific precision and recall, hold out conversations and users from their test set, provide prompts and major training hyperparameters, and report approximate compute requirements.

The paper is clearly organized, and its figures and tables make the construction and evaluation procedures understandable. Review based on the complete manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/92f7af56b7494b6486cbf3aaa88dca32/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The strongest claim—improved alignment with actual users—is not independently established. Preferences are summarized by GPT-4, preferred responses are frequently generated by GPT-4, and the main WildFeedback evaluation again uses GPT-4 with those same summaries as checklists. This creates a substantial self-confirming evaluation loop. Neither originating users nor independent humans evaluate the trained models' outputs against their actual preferences.

The human validation does not resolve this circularity. For checklist-guided evaluation, GPT–human agreement is only 57.14% with κ=0.372; human–human agreement is itself only 63.27% with κ=0.436. Calling GPT-4's performance relatively high or on par with humans overstates weak-to-moderate reliability. Moreover, annotators judge compliance with inferred checklists, not whether the original user would prefer the response.

Feedback identification is imperfect where it matters most: DSAT recall is 48.4% and κ is 0.504, based on only 50 conversations. This likely induces substantial selection and labeling bias, yet downstream sensitivity to detector errors is not analyzed.

Preference-pair construction is insufficiently specified. The manuscript does not clearly explain how SAT-only conversations contribute, how 13,582 DSAT conversations yield 20,281 GPT-4 pairs, how multiple feedback events are handled, or precisely how prompts and preferred responses are generated. Appendix A.2 covers preference extraction but not the complete response-generation procedure.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: the dataset is merely said to be available soon, and important details are missing, including exact data splits, generation decoding settings, random seeds, embedding model and clustering configuration, deduplication criteria, moderation/filtering outcomes, and complete hyperparameter-selection procedures.

The results lack uncertainty estimates, significance tests, and repeated training runs despite claims of significant and consistent improvement. Some WildFeedback configurations do not outperform their matched UltraFeedback counterpart on every metric—for example, Phi-3 and Qwen-2 GPT-4 variants—so the narrative is stronger than the reported evidence.

All general benchmarks also rely on LLM judges, leaving potential shared-judge bias. A blinded human evaluation of trained-model outputs, preferably involving the source users or independently elicited user-specific preferences, is needed before the central alignment claim is sound. Safety is handled only through an instruction and moderation filter, without an empirical safety evaluation.

Overall, the idea and initial evidence are promising, but the circular evaluation, low validation agreement, incomplete construction details, and unavailable resource prevent a clear Findings recommendation. These concerns appear addressable in a focused revision, making the submission borderline for Findings rather than fundamentally unsound.

strengths: The paper addresses an important ACL problem: learning preferences from natural, multi-turn user–LLM interactions rather than relying entirely on hired annotators or synthetic prompts.
The proposed pipeline—detecting satisfaction signals, inferring preferences, constructing preference pairs, and using preference-specific evaluation checklists—is intuitive and potentially useful.

The experiments cover three model families and several established benchmarks. Some improvements over the instruction-tuned base models are sizable, including Phi-3 increasing from 24.3 to 34.9 on length-controlled AlpacaEval 2 and from 15.4 to 32.4 on Arena-Hard.

The authors attempt to validate intermediate components with human annotations, provide prompts and training hyperparameters, and acknowledge selection bias and malicious user preferences as limitations.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved alignment with actual users is not adequately established. Users never assess the synthesized preferred responses. GPT-4 infers each preference, generates or filters preferred responses, and subsequently judges outputs using that inferred preference. This circular design mainly establishes consistency with GPT-4's interpretation of users, not satisfaction of the original users.

The checklist evaluation is too unreliable to support the principal alignment claim: GPT-4–human agreement is only 57.14% with kappa 0.372, while human–human agreement is 63.27% with kappa 0.436. Characterizing this as relatively high or on par overstates the evidence. No independent, blinded human or user evaluation of the trained models is reported.

Preference-pair construction is heavily confounded. In WF GPT-4, an original ChatGPT response is contrasted with a newly generated GPT-4o response, so teacher quality can explain the gains independently of feedback conditioning. Essential controls are missing, including generation from the same prompts without inferred preferences, shuffled preferences, and comparisons controlling for prompt distribution and multi-turn context length.

Important construction details are unclear. The paper specifies how DSAT-triggering responses become dispreferred examples but not how SAT examples produce complete pairs. The appendix provides a preference-extraction prompt rather than the complete preferred-response generation procedure. Filtering, moderation, decoding, clustering, deduplication, and hyperparameter-selection details are also insufficient.

The feedback detector has only 48.4% recall and 61.2 F1 for DSAT, based on merely 50 conversations. The multi-label agreement methodology is unclear, and annotator qualifications, compensation, language coverage, and label prevalence are unreported. Detector errors directly determine the resulting training corpus.

The held-out evaluation deliberately selects preferences similar to others in their clusters and tasks resembling the training data, then evaluates with the same GPT-4-derived checklists. This favors common, learnable preferences and does not substantiate claims about diverse or evolving real-world users.

The benchmark evidence lacks uncertainty estimates, significance tests, and repeated runs. Results are not uniformly superior: Qwen-2 WF GPT-4 trails UF GPT-4 on length-controlled AlpacaEval 2 and MT-Bench. Thus, claims of significant and consistent superiority exceed the reported evidence.

Reproducibility is inadequate for Findings. The dataset is only promised as 'available soon,' no code or artifact link is supplied, exact data and model snapshots are missing, and the undisclosed hyperparameter grid search cannot be reconstructed. Dependence on proprietary APIs makes precise versioning and released intermediate outputs especially important.

The safety and ethics analysis is insufficient for preference data mined from user conversations. A generic safety instruction and unspecified moderation filtering are not empirically validated, while sensitive-data memorization, demographic and linguistic representation, user identification through hashes, and downstream safety effects are not meaningfully assessed.

The direction and public-benchmark gains justify revision rather than abandonment, but independent human validation, deconfounded ablations, complete methodological documentation, statistical analysis, and released artifacts are needed before the paper meets the soundness and reproducibility threshold for Findings. These revisions appear feasible for a subsequent cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem and presents an appealing practical direction: extracting naturally occurring feedback from multi-turn user–LLM conversations instead of relying entirely on purpose-built annotation.

The end-to-end framework is clearly motivated and combines feedback detection, preference-pair construction, model training, and instance-specific evaluation. Applying it to 148,715 WildChat conversations yields a substantial resource of up to 20,281 preference examples.

Experiments cover three model families and include both GPT-4-generated and on-policy data, plus comparisons against off-the-shelf models and regenerated UltraFeedback baselines. The generally strong improvements on AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard, and MT-Bench provide credible evidence that the resulting training data can improve broad instruction-following performance.

The authors make useful efforts to validate intermediate components with human annotation, report agreement and classification statistics rather than relying solely on anecdotal examples, and openly acknowledge selection bias and unsafe or malicious user preferences.
The paper is readable, well organized, and supplies prompts, principal training hyperparameters, resource estimates, dataset statistics, and privacy information in the appendices.
weaknesses: The evidence does not adequately establish the central claim of improved alignment with actual user preferences. GPT-4 detects feedback, summarizes preferences, often generates the preferred response, filters on-policy pairs, and judges the principal WildFeedback evaluation. This dependence creates substantial circularity, and no held-out users directly evaluate the fine-tuned models' outputs.

The human validation of checklist-guided evaluation is weak: GPT-4 reaches only 57.14% raw agreement and kappa 0.372, while human–human agreement is itself only 63.27% with kappa 0.436. Describing this as relatively high or on par with humans does not make the resulting metric a reliable proxy for user preference, especially because it supports a central claim.

The WildFeedback test-set construction favors preferences near cluster centers and tasks similar to the training set. Although users and conversations are reportedly separated, this deliberately in-distribution selection makes the comparison against UltraFeedback susceptible to dataset-domain matching and does not test generalization to diverse or idiosyncratic users.

Several claims overstate the reported results. WildFeedback does not consistently outperform UltraFeedback in Table 3—for example, Qwen-2 WF GPT-4 trails UF GPT-4 on length-controlled AlpacaEval and MT-Bench, and multiple raw win-rate comparisons favor UltraFeedback. No confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated training runs, or judge-variance estimates support the repeated use of “significantly.”

The preference-construction description is insufficiently precise, particularly regarding how SAT cases contribute preferred/dispreferred responses and how multiple feedback signals within a conversation become examples. Moreover, all GPT-4-generated pairs are retained even though Figure 2 indicates a nontrivial proportion of intended preferred responses tie or lose under the paper's own evaluator.

Feedback identification has only 48.4% recall for DSAT, so a large and potentially systematic portion of naturally occurring dissatisfaction is missed. The resulting selection bias, together with the much higher incidence of negative than positive feedback, limits claims that the dataset captures broad or diverse human values.

Important controls are missing. The experiments do not isolate the effects of natural feedback from multi-turn context, prompt/domain distribution, GPT-4 preference-conditioned rewriting, filtering, or response length. Consequently, the benchmark gains demonstrate the utility of the complete pipeline but not that in-situ feedback is the decisive cause.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate for a clear Findings recommendation: the dataset is only promised as “available soon,” and no code, checkpoints, fixed splits, random seeds, generation parameters, moderation/filtering details, or complete hyperparameter-search specification are provided. A revised paper with released artifacts, independent human evaluation, uncertainty estimates, and more careful claims could plausibly reach Findings.
